lights.name: St. George Reef Light Station
lights.coord_source: US Coast Guard Light List Vol. VI 2025, LLNR 561 (41-50-14.000N 124-22-32.000W); cross-checked against corrected UTM 10/385800/4632400 in NRHP nomination 93001373
lights.first_lit: First-order lens installed August 1892; station in operation by October 1892 (NRHP nomination 93001373, which quotes the 1892 Annual Report of the Light-House Board; the nomination dates a keeper's death 17 Oct 1893 'hardly a year after the station began operation'). The commonly cited day, 20 October 1892, is tertiary-level only in this survey.
lights.established_structures: Single granite tower on Northwest Seal Rock, built 1883-1891/92 on an elliptical concrete-and-granite pier; keepers withdrawn and station disestablished 13 May 1975 (nomination); relit as a restored private aid (Light List 2025, 'Restored historic light').
lights.optic: First-order Fresnel, 1892, flashing alternately red and white (NRHP nomination; USCG Historian's Office). Lens removed 1975 to the Del Norte County Historical Society museum (nomination).
lights.why_built: Marks the offshore reef where the steamer Brother Jonathan sank in 1865; the USCG Historian's Office narrative states the light 'marks the site of the tragic sinking of the steamer Brother Jonathan.' Land reserved by President Andrew Johnson after a May 1866 Light-House Board draft; construction 1883-1891 under Capt. A.H. Payson and then A. Ballantyne, total cost about $704,634-$726,000 (nomination quoting the 1892 Annual Report).
lights.automated: Never conventionally automated on station; USCG table marks 'automated' without a year. Disestablished 13 May 1975 and replaced by a lighted buoy.
lights.deactivated: 13 May 1975 (NRHP nomination); relit as a private aid in the 2000s-2010s (Light List 2025 carries it as LLNR 561, Fl W 12s, 'Restored historic light'; relight year 2012 is tertiary only).
lights.fate: Standing; owned by Del Norte County per USCG page; maintained by the St. George Reef Lighthouse Preservation Society (tertiary; not independently verified). First-order lens displayed at Del Norte County Historical Society, Crescent City.
lights.nrhp: Listed 1993-12-09, ref 93001373, under Light Stations of California MPS (NRIS dataset 2026-05-22).
lights.keepers_note: On 17 October 1893, about a year after operations began, the first assistant keeper lost his life at the station (NRHP nomination); the USCG narrative adds that several men were injured or killed over the years transferring to the rock by small boat, and describes an 1923 storm that tore the donkey-engine house from its foundation 70 feet above the water.
lights.summary: The most expensive American lighthouse of its century, St. George Reef took eight working seasons (1883-1891) to raise on a wave-swept rock six miles off Point St. George, using 1,339 dressed granite blocks quarried near the Mad River. Its first-order flashing lens went into service in 1892 and warned shipping off the reef that had claimed the Brother Jonathan in 1865. The Coast Guard disestablished the station in May 1975 in favor of a buoy; the tower still stands and again shows a private light.

lights.name: Battery Point Light (Crescent City)
lights.coord_source: US Coast Guard Light List Vol. VI 2025, LLNR 555 (41-44-39.000N 124-12-11.000W); NPS NRHP GIS point 41.74403,-124.20309 agrees
lights.first_lit: First exhibited 10 December 1856 (USC&GS Pacific Coast Pilot, 4th ed. 1889: 'first exhibited on the 10th of December, 1856'; the same passage notes it was not shown for a period beginning April 1860).
lights.established_structures: 1856 Cape Cod-type dwelling with integral tower on Battery Point islet, one of the first West Coast lighthouses; still the original structure. Automatic light installed July 1953; leased to Del Norte County; light deactivated 1965-1982 (USCG); relit as a private aid 10 December 1982 (NRHP nomination).
lights.optic: Fourth-order Fresnel, 1856 (USCG Historian's Office).
lights.why_built: One of the first cohort of Pacific coast lighthouses authorized in the early 1850s to serve the gold-rush coastal trade; Crescent City was one of only two real harbors (with Humboldt Bay) on the redwood north coast (Bookwalter, Light Stations of California MPS, 1989).
lights.automated: 1953 (USCG; nomination: automatic light installed July 1953).
lights.deactivated: 1965-1982 (USCG table); relit 10 December 1982 as a private aid (nomination). Active today as LLNR 555, Fl W 30s, 'Restored historic light.'
lights.fate: Standing; museum operated with Del Norte County (county lease from 1953 per USCG); tidal-island access.
lights.nrhp: Listed 1983-09-15 as 'Cresent City Lighthouse' [sic], ref 83001177 (NRIS dataset).
lights.summary: Battery Point is one of the survivors of California's first generation of lighthouses: a brick tower rising through a granite Cape Cod dwelling on a tidal islet at Crescent City, first exhibited 10 December 1856. Automated in 1953 and dark from 1965, it was relit as a private aid on 10 December 1982 and now operates as a county museum still showing a light.

lights.name: Trinidad Head Light Station
lights.coord_source: US Coast Guard Light List Vol. VI 2025, LLNR 525 (41-03-06.869N 124-09-05.242W)
lights.first_lit: 1871 (USC&GS Coast Pilot 1889: 'first exhibited in 1871'; NRHP nomination 91001098 and USCG concur on 1871; the customary day, 1 December 1871, is tertiary-level in this survey).
lights.established_structures: 1871 square pyramidal brick tower, still standing and basically unchanged; 1898 bell house with 4,000-lb fog bell; original Victorian dwelling razed late 1960s for a Coast Guard triplex (USCG). Original 4th-order lens removed 1947 and installed 1948-49 in a memorial replica tower in the town of Trinidad (USCG; NRHP nomination says the original lens was installed in the replica in 1948).
lights.optic: Fourth-order Fresnel, 1871; replaced 1947 by a 375 mm optic (USCG).
lights.why_built: Served Trinidad Harbor and the north-coast lumber trade; the nomination's significance statement runs from 1871 under commerce, transportation and maritime history, within the doghole-port economy described in the Light Stations of California MPS.
lights.automated: February 1974 (USCG).
lights.deactivated: Never; active USCG aid (Light List 2025, Oc W 4s, HORN).
lights.fate: Standing; active aid with Coast Guard housing on the head; original lens and bell displayed at the town's memorial lighthouse.
lights.nrhp: Listed 1991-09-03, ref 91001098, Light Stations of California MPS (NRIS).
lights.keepers_note: In 1913 the keeper reported a freak wave that struck the 196-foot headland: 'The sea shot up the face of the bluff and over it, until the solid sea seemed to me to be on a level with where I stood in the lantern... The whole point between the tower and the bluff was buried in water' (quoted on the USCG Historian's Office page).
lights.summary: A squat brick tower of 1871 whose modest 20-foot height is multiplied by Trinidad Head's 196-foot cliff, this light covered the crowded lumber-schooner harbor at Trinidad. It keeps its original station arrangement minus the razed Victorian dwelling, and its 1871 lens survives in a replica tower in town. It remains an active Coast Guard aid, automated in 1974.

lights.name: Table Bluff Light Station
lights.coord_source: USGS GNIS DomesticNames_CA, feature 235952 'Table Bluff' (Cliff, Humboldt County) - coordinate is for the bluff, not a published lighthouse position
lights.first_lit: 1892 (USCG Historian's Office: 'In 1892 the Lighthouse Service constructed a light station on Table Bluff'; NPS inventory: 'TABLE BLUFF LIGHT (1892)'). The customary day, 31 October 1892, is tertiary-level only.
lights.established_structures: 1892 Stick-style keeper's dwelling with attached square wooden tower (near-twin of San Luis Obispo), duplex quarters and fog-signal building; most station buildings razed during and after WWII, leaving the tower and fog-signal building; the quarters portion of the lighthouse itself was razed leaving only the tower (USCG). The MPS context groups its fanciful Stick-style plans with San Luis Obispo and Ballast Point.
lights.optic: Fourth-order rotating Fresnel; in 1953 replaced by a fixed smaller lens and the 4th-order optic shipped to Old Point Loma for museum display; the later lens went to the Smithsonian on discontinuation (USCG; the page gives the replacement lens inconsistently as '3 1/2 order' and '2 1/2 order').
lights.why_built: Replaced the 1856 Humboldt Harbor light on the sinking, low North Spit, 'for many years... criticized as being too low' (USCG); the 1889 Coast Pilot already records that 'it has been proposed to remove the Humboldt Light-house to this bluff.'
lights.automated: 1953; fog signal discontinued the same year (USCG).
lights.deactivated: 1975 per the USCG narrative ('In 1975 the light was discontinued and the property transferred to GSA and sold'); the same page's data table says deactivated 1961 - conflict noted.
lights.fate: Station property sold; tower reportedly relocated to Woodley Island, Eureka, in the 1980s (tertiary, not verified in located records).
lights.nrhp: Not found in the NRIS listed-properties dataset (2026-05-22); apparently never listed.
lights.summary: Table Bluff took over Humboldt Bay's seacoast light in 1892 from the failing North Spit station, placing a Stick-style dwelling-tower on the high bluff south of the bay. The Navy added a radio station in 1906 and the site swelled with beach-patrol and radio-compass functions in WWII, after which most of the original complex was demolished. Automated in 1953, the light was discontinued in the 1970s and the property sold.

lights.name: Humboldt Harbor Light (1856)
lights.coord_source: No published coordinate located. The 1889 Coast Pilot places it 'on the North Spit or Peninsula, three-quarters of a mile north of the entrance to the bay and about midway between the bay and the sea-shores.'
lights.first_lit: First exhibited 20 December 1856 (USC&GS Pacific Coast Pilot, 4th ed. 1889: 'The Light was first exhibited on December 20, 1856').
lights.established_structures: 1856 one-and-a-half-story brick keeper's dwelling with a conical tower rising 21 feet above the roof, plastered and painted white (Coast Pilot 1889). Superseded by Table Bluff in 1892; the MPS context cites it as the type-case of a Cape Cod design failing 'when constructed on the sinking sands of Humboldt Bay.'
lights.optic: Fourth-order Fresnel, fixed white (Coast Pilot 1889). The third-order lens originally intended for Humboldt Harbor was diverted to Old Point Loma in 1855 (USCG Historian's Office, Old Point Loma entry).
lights.why_built: Humboldt Bay was one of the two harbors of the redwood coast and the outlet of its lumber trade; one of the first cohort of Pacific lighthouses funded in the early 1850s (MPS context; Coast Pilot 1889 notes the excessive fog at the site).
lights.automated: Never; replaced instead.
lights.deactivated: 1892, when Table Bluff was established (USCG Table Bluff entry).
lights.fate: Abandoned after 1892; ruins later lost (final demolition/collapse date not verified in located sources).
lights.nrhp: Not listed (not in NRIS dataset).
lights.summary: Lit on 20 December 1856, the Humboldt Harbor light was a brick Cape Cod dwelling-tower planted on the low, unstable North Spit of Humboldt Bay. Sited too low and plagued by fog and settling ground, it was criticized for decades; the Coast Survey was already reporting a proposal to move the light to Table Bluff in 1889, and the 1892 Table Bluff station superseded it.

lights.name: Cape Mendocino Light Station
lights.coord_source: USGS GNIS DomesticNames_CA, feature 254709 'Cape Mendocino' (Cape) - coordinate is for the cape; the tower stood on its seaward face 422 ft above the sea (USCG). Tower relocated 1998 to Mal Coombs Park, Shelter Cove.
lights.first_lit: First exhibited 1 December 1868 (Coast Pilot 1889: 'The Light was first exhibited December 1, 1868'; USCG concurs: 'activated on December 1, 1868').
lights.established_structures: 1868 prefabricated 16-sided cast-iron pyramidal tower, 43 ft, one of the highest lights in the U.S. at 422 ft above the sea; the MPS groups its iron-plate prefabrication with Point Reyes. Automated 1951; abandoned 1970s; tower dismantled and re-erected 1998 at Mal Coombs Park, Shelter Cove (USCG).
lights.optic: First-order Fresnel, revolving (Coast Pilot 1889; USCG). Lens moved 1948 to a replica tower at the Humboldt County Fairgrounds, Ferndale (USCG).
lights.why_built: Cape Mendocino is the westernmost turning point of the California coast and its most prominent seamark for coastwise traffic; a first-order coastal light of the post-Civil War expansion (MPS context; Coast Pilot describes it as the abrupt termination of a mountainous ridge).
lights.deactivated: Station abandoned in the 1970s (USCG table: 'Deactivated: 1970s'); a minor light on the site continued later per tertiary sources (Wikipedia infobox gives 2013), not verified.
lights.fate: Tower preserved at Shelter Cove (Cape Mendocino Lighthouse Preservation Society, per USCG); lens at Ferndale fairgrounds.
lights.nrhp: Not listed (not in NRIS dataset).
lights.summary: Lit on 1 December 1868, Cape Mendocino's prefabricated cast-iron tower stood 422 feet above the Pacific on the state's westernmost cape, its first-order flash marking the great turn of the coast. Automated in 1951 and abandoned by the 1970s, the little tower was dismantled in 1998 and rebuilt at Shelter Cove, while its lens has sat in Ferndale since 1948.

lights.name: Punta Gorda Light Station
lights.coord_source: NRHP nomination 76000483, UTM zone 10 / 385630 E / 4455700 N (NAD27), converted; GNIS cape feature 231095 (40.2612,-124.3628) is the headland ~2 km north
lights.first_lit: 15 January 1912: 'The fog-signal... went into operation on June 22, 1911; and a half a year later, on January 15, 1912, the station's light shown for the first time' (NRHP nomination 76000483).
lights.established_structures: Built 1910-11: reinforced-concrete light building (a squat two-story block), concrete oil house, wooden fog-signal building, three two-story frame keepers' dwellings, shops and barn strung along the beach bench (nomination). Light extinguished 15 February 1951; BLM burned all buildings except the lighthouse and oil house after 1960s squatting (nomination; USCG).
lights.optic: Fourth-order lens with incandescent oil-vapor lamp, focal plane 75 ft, visible 14 miles; electric lamp only from the 1940s (nomination). USCG table calls it a 'fourth order, bulls eye 1912.' Whereabouts of the lens unknown (USCG).
lights.why_built: Ten ships sank or stranded near Punta Gorda 1895-1907, ending with the Columbia, which collided with a lumber schooner on 12 July 1907 with 77 lives lost; 'this disaster was undoubtedly the impetus,' and Congress appropriated $60,000 in 1908 (nomination). The steamer St. Paul's 1905 boiler still lay a few hundred feet from the construction site.
lights.automated: Unknown/none - USCG marks automation 'UNK'; the station was simply discontinued.
lights.deactivated: 15 February 1951 (nomination; USCG gives 1951).
lights.fate: Lighthouse and oil house stand on the remote Lost Coast; transferred to BLM 16 January 1963 (nomination). The 2016 USCG page instead says California Dept. of Parks and Recreation - conflict unresolved (the site is commonly described as BLM King Range NCA).
lights.nrhp: Listed 1976-09-01, ref 76000483 (NRIS dataset serial; ArcGIS layer lacks it).
lights.keepers_note: One of the loneliest posts in the district: supplies came by boat until 1915 and afterward by horse and wagon from Petrolia, ten and a half miles away, with creeks cutting the route off for seven months a year (nomination). After closure, squatters occupied the quarters until BLM evicted them and burned every building but the concrete pair (USCG).
lights.summary: The 'Alcatraz of lighthouses' on the Lost Coast was built after the Columbia disaster of 1907 capped a dozen years of wrecks below Cape Mendocino; its fog sirens sounded from June 1911 and the fourth-order light first shone on 15 January 1912. Nearly roadless its whole working life, the station was extinguished on 15 February 1951, and only the small concrete lighthouse and oil house survived the BLM's burn of the abandoned quarters.

lights.name: Point Cabrillo Light Station
lights.coord_source: US Coast Guard Light List Vol. VI 2025, LLNR 450 (39-20-54.905N 123-49-33.828W)
lights.first_lit: 10 June 1909: 'Its first beam of light shown on June 10, 1909' (NRHP nomination 91001092; USCG concurs on 1909).
lights.established_structures: 1909 octagonal wooden tower integral with its fog-signal building, plus keepers' dwellings; 'with the exception of a small barn all original buildings stand unaltered' (USCG). Air diaphone supertyfone installed 1935.
lights.optic: Third-order Fresnel, 1909, still in the tower at listing ('architecturally intact including its original 3rd order Fresnel lens,' nomination).
lights.why_built: Filled the dark gap on the Mendocino lumber coast between Point Arena and Cape Mendocino, serving the doghole-schooner redwood trade; land acquired for the station in 1906 (nomination; MPS context counts ~100 doghole ports in Sonoma-Mendocino-Humboldt).
lights.deactivated: Never; active (Light List 2025, Fl W 10s, emergency light provision).
lights.fate: Standing and restored as Point Cabrillo Light Station State Historic Park (California DPR; USCG page notes nature-preserve restoration).
lights.nrhp: Listed 1991-09-03, ref 91001092, Light Stations of California MPS (NRIS).
lights.summary: Point Cabrillo, first lit on 10 June 1909, is a wooden light-and-fog-signal building of the Lighthouse Service's late frame idiom, built for the redwood doghole trade out of Mendocino and Fort Bragg. Its original third-order lens survived automation in 1973, and the station complex, nearly complete, is now a California state historic park.

lights.name: Point Arena Light Station
lights.coord_source: US Coast Guard Light List Vol. VI 2025, LLNR 420 (38-57-17.139N 123-44-26.214W)
lights.first_lit: First tower first exhibited 1 May 1870 (Coast Pilot 1889: first-order light 'first exhibited May 1, 1870'); replacement tower lit 1908 (NRHP nomination 90002189 significant dates 1870/1908; USCG).
lights.established_structures: 1870 brick conical tower, 100 ft (Coast Pilot); wrecked by the 18 April 1906 earthquake and torn down; replaced 1908 by the first reinforced-concrete lighthouse tower in the nation, built by a San Francisco chimney contractor, with 1908 auxiliary buildings (MPS context; nomination).
lights.optic: First-order Fresnel 1870; first-order rotating Fresnel in the 1908 tower (USCG). Lens since removed from the tower for ground display on loan from the Coast Guard (USCG).
lights.why_built: Marked the prominent Point Arena headland and its dangerous outlying reef for the coastwise lumber and passenger trade north of San Francisco (Coast Pilot 1889 landfall description; MPS context).
lights.automated: 1977, when the crew was removed (USCG).
lights.deactivated: Never; active (Light List 2025, Fl W 15s).
lights.fate: Standing; transferred to the nonprofit Point Arena Lighthouse Keepers, Inc. (USCG); museum and vacation rentals (NPS inventory).
lights.nrhp: Listed 1991-07-16, ref 90002189, under the Point Arena MPS (NRIS).
lights.summary: Point Arena's first-order light of 1 May 1870 stood only 36 years before the 1906 San Andreas rupture, whose trace passes just offshore, shattered the brick tower. Its 1908 replacement, a slim reinforced-concrete shaft raised by a San Francisco chimney firm, was the first concrete lighthouse in the country and the model for many later towers. Automated in 1977, it is now run by a local nonprofit.

lights.name: Point Reyes Light Station
lights.coord_source: US Coast Guard Light List Vol. VI 2025, LLNR 385 (37-59-44.205N 123-01-23.413W)
lights.first_lit: First exhibited 1 December 1870 (Coast Pilot 1889: first-order lens 'first exhibited December 1, 1870').
lights.established_structures: 1870 sixteen-sided forged-iron-plate tower bolted to rock 294 ft above the sea, reached by 304 steps from the headland (USCG 1962 pamphlet quote); fog-signal building, engine room and later quarters above. A modern automated beacon took over in 1975; the historic tower is preserved.
lights.optic: First-order rotating Fresnel, 1870 (Coast Pilot 1889; USCG table).
lights.why_built: Point Reyes forms the seaward hazard of the Gulf of the Farallones on the approach to San Francisco, and is by official record the windiest and foggiest station on the Pacific coast (USCG pamphlet, 1962); a first-order headland light of the post-war program (MPS).
lights.automated: 1975, when the Coast Guard installed automated equipment and retired the historic light (USCG table: automated/deactivated 1975).
lights.deactivated: Historic lens light retired 1975; the station remains an active aid via the adjacent automated beacon (Light List 2025, Fl W 5s, horn).
lights.fate: Transferred to the National Park Service; exhibit within Point Reyes National Seashore (USCG; NPS inventory).
lights.nrhp: Listed 1991-09-03, ref 91001100, Light Stations of California MPS (NRIS).
lights.keepers_note: The Coast Guard's own 1962 description: 'Point Reyes is, by official records, the windiest and foggiest on the Pacific Coast... few years pass that do not see violent gales of 75 to 100 mph strike the area,' with keepers descending 304 steps to the lantern (quoted on the USCG page).
lights.summary: Set into the cliff-face 294 feet above the surf because fog smothers the 600-foot headland above, Point Reyes first showed its first-order flash on 1 December 1870. Its iron-plate tower and clockwork lens served through a century of gales before automation in 1975, and the station now anchors the maritime story of Point Reyes National Seashore.

lights.name: Farallon Islands Light (Southeast Farallon)
lights.coord_source: US Coast Guard Light List Vol. VI 2025, LLNR 355 (37-41-57.105N 123-00-06.615W); the 1889 Coast Pilot gives 37 41 51 N, 123 00 07 W for islet summit
lights.first_lit: 1855 per USCG Historian's Office and NPS inventory ('Station Established: 1855 / First Lit: 1855'); the frequently cited first exhibition of the first-order lens on 1 January 1856 is tertiary-level in this survey. The first tower of 1853-54 had to be rebuilt before the lens fit.
lights.established_structures: Brick-lined stone conical tower on the 360-ft summit of Southeast Farallon, built 1855 with brick carried up the rock 'in bundles of four and five on the backs of men' (USCG); lantern room later removed and replaced by an automatic beacon on the tower (USCG photo captions show the tower with and without lantern).
lights.optic: First-order Fresnel, 1855 (USCG table).
lights.why_built: Guarded the deadly outer approach to Gold Rush San Francisco; the USCG narrative cites clippers such as the Golden City, detained five days off the Farallones in fog in 1852, as evidence of the need.
lights.deactivated: Never; active (Light List 2025, Fl W 15s, white conical tower).
lights.fate: Active aid within the Farallon National Wildlife Refuge (NPS inventory); island research station.
lights.nrhp: The islands were listed as the 'Farallone Islands' district, ref 77000332, on 1977-03-08 (NRIS); the lighthouse is within that listing.
lights.keepers_note: For years a station mule - at one point 'the oldest inhabitant' - carried supplies up the rock; commercial egg-gathering for the San Francisco market and sealing went on around the keepers until the federal government stopped both (USCG page).
lights.summary: The Farallones light, raised in 1855 on the granite peak of Southeast Farallon, was among the first cohort of Pacific lights and among the hardest built, with every brick packed uphill by hand. Its first-order lens covered the fog-bound outer approach to San Francisco for over a century; the tower, automated in 1972 and stripped of its lantern, still flashes over a national wildlife refuge.

lights.name: Point Montara Light Station
alt_names: Point Montara Fog Signal and Light Station
lights.coord_source: US Coast Guard Light List Vol. VI 2025, LLNR 335 (37-32-11.324N 122-31-09.447W)
lights.first_lit: Fog-signal station established February 1875 (USCG pamphlet); 'Point Montara served exclusively as a fog-signal station until 1900 when a small post beacon was added. In 1912 a 4th order Fresnel lens was put atop a wooden tower' (NRHP nomination 91001094; the same document elsewhere says a beacon was added in 1902 - internal conflict noted). Present tower erected 1928.
lights.established_structures: 1875 fog-signal station; 1900 (or 1902) post light; 1912 wooden Fresnel tower, demolished 1928; 1928 conical cast-iron/steel tower that still stands (nomination; USCG 'Point Montara Light... 1928').
lights.optic: Fourth-order Fresnel, 1912, transferred to the 1928 tower; later replaced by a modern airway-type beacon (nomination).
lights.why_built: Wrecks on the fog-bound ledges south of the Golden Gate: the nomination cites a shore ledge wreck in 1868 and the ship Acuelo gutted below Mt. Montara in November 1872 as the impetus for the fog signal.
lights.automated: 1970 (USCG table).
lights.deactivated: Never; active (Light List 2025, Fl W 5s).
lights.fate: Standing; station is a youth hostel licensed to California State Parks (USCG).

lights.summary: Montara began in February 1875 as a fog-signal station answering the wrecks on the ledges south of San Francisco, and only grew a light by stages: a small beacon around 1900, a fourth-order lens on a wooden tower in 1912, and the present little cast-iron tower in 1928. lights.summary: Año Nuevo was a fog station first and a lighthouse second: the government set a steam whistle on the islet in 1872 and added a five-story tower only in 1890. lights.name: Santa Cruz Light Station
lights.coord_source: US Coast Guard Light List Vol. VI 2025, LLNR 305 'Santa Cruz Light' (36-57-05.340N 122-01-36.360W) - the modern Mark Abbott Memorial tower near the original site; the 1869 lighthouse stood on the same point (moved 300 ft inland in 1878 for erosion, USCG)

lights.established_structures: 1869 wooden dwelling with square tower at Point Santa Cruz; moved 300 ft inland 1878 due to erosion; light discontinued 1941; structure sold 1948 and razed in May 1948 (USCG). Brick Mark Abbott Memorial Lighthouse built near the site by the Abbott family after their son drowned surfing in 1965, using the lantern room from the Oakland Harbor Light; it carries today's Santa Cruz Light (USCG; Light List).
lights.optic: Fifth-order Fresnel, fixed red (Coast Pilot 1889); a fourth-order lens installed 1909 (USCG).
lights.why_built: Served the narrow-gauge port and coastal trade of Santa Cruz on Monterey Bay (MPS context lists Santa Cruz among the narrow-gauge outlets; Coast Pilot's sailing directions key on the light for the wharves).
lights.automated: No - the original station was keeper-run to the end (last keeper Arthur Anderson until 1941, USCG).
lights.deactivated: 1941 (USCG); the present Santa Cruz Light (Fl W 5s) is the memorial tower, home of the Santa Cruz Surfing Museum.
lights.fate: Original razed May 1948; successor brick tower stands as museum and active aid.
lights.nrhp: Not listed (not in NRIS dataset).
lights.keepers_note: Laura Hecox succeeded her father A.A. Hecox as keeper in 1883 and served until 1916 - a 33-year tenure; only three keepers ran the light in its whole life (USCG). Her natural-history collection seeded the Santa Cruz city museum (tertiary; not verified).

Discontinued in 1941 and razed in 1948, it was succeeded in spirit and function by the Mark Abbott Memorial Lighthouse, a 1960s brick memorial that now carries the official Santa Cruz Light and a surfing museum.

lights.name: Point Pinos Light Station
lights.coord_source: US Coast Guard Light List Vol. VI 2025, LLNR 290 (36-38-00.165N 121-56-01.432W)
lights.first_lit: 1855 (USCG: established/first lit 1855; NRHP nomination 77000312: 'completed in 1855, shortly after Alcatraz Light'). The customary day, 1 February 1855, is tertiary-level in this survey. Oldest continuously operating lighthouse on the West Coast (USCG).
lights.established_structures: 1855 granite Cape Cod dwelling with central conical brick tower - the original structure still in service; the third-order lens likewise original and operational (USCG; Coast Pilot 1889 describes the gray granite dwelling and round white tower).
lights.optic: Third-order Fresnel, purchased in France, in continuous use ('Even the original lens is still operational,' USCG; nomination concurs).
lights.why_built: Marked the southern entrance of Monterey Bay for the port of Monterey, one of the first cohort of eight Pacific lighthouses of the 1850s (MPS context; Coast Pilot).
lights.deactivated: Never; active (Light List 2025, Oc W 4s).
lights.fate: Standing; light transferred to the City of Pacific Grove in 2006; museum (USCG).
lights.keepers_note: First keeper Charles Layton died in office; local citizens petitioned the Lighthouse Board to appoint his widow Charlotte Layton keeper, and another woman, Emily Fish, later held the post; Robert Louis Stevenson visited and wrote about the light (USCG page).
lights.summary: Point Pinos, lit in 1855, is the oldest continuously operating lighthouse on the Pacific coast of the United States, still showing its original French third-order lens from the original granite Cape Cod building. Its early keepers included two notable women, Charlotte Layton and Emily Fish. Automated in 1975, it now belongs to the City of Pacific Grove.

lights.name: Point Sur Light Station
lights.coord_source: US Coast Guard Light List Vol. VI 2025, LLNR 280 (36-18-22.513N 121-54-05.621W)

lights.name: San Luis Obispo Light Station (Port Harford)
lights.coord_source: US Coast Guard Light List Vol. VI 2025, LLNR 225 (35-09-36.840N 120-45-37.822W)
lights.first_lit: Completed 30 June 1890: 'the station was not completed until June 30, 1890' (NRHP nomination 91001093); USCG dates establishment and first lighting 1890.
lights.established_structures: 1890 Stick-style (Victorian) dwelling with attached 40-ft square tower - the only survivor of the identical 1890 trio with Ballast Point and Table Bluff (MPS: 'Only San Luis Obispo remains today'); fog-signal building with 10-inch steam whistle (USCG).
lights.optic: Fourth-order Fresnel (USCG); replaced by a modern beacon in 1969, lens moved 1976 to the San Luis Obispo County Historical Society (USCG).
lights.why_built: Port Harford (Avila) was the coastal outlet of San Luis Obispo and 'one of the most active ports between San Francisco and San Diego,' with no light in the 94 miles between Point Arguello and Piedras Blancas; the sinking of the steamer Queen of the Pacific on 30 April 1888 clinched the appropriation (nomination).
lights.deactivated: 1975 as a staffed lighthouse; the site still shows a light (Light List 2025, Fl W 5s, lighted 24 hours).
lights.fate: Standing; restored by the Point San Luis Lighthouse Keepers as a museum (USCG; the Harbor District stewardship is a tertiary detail not verified).
lights.nrhp: Listed 1991-09-03, ref 91001093, Light Stations of California MPS (NRIS).
lights.summary: The Port Harford light of 30 June 1890 answered the Queen of the Pacific's 1888 sinking and the long dark gap of the south-central coast, planting a gingerbread Stick-style dwelling-tower on Point San Luis. It is the only one of its three identical 1890 sisters still standing, its fourth-order lens now in county museum hands and its buildings restored for visitors.

lights.name: Point Arguello Light Station
lights.coord_source: US Coast Guard Light List Vol. VI 2025, LLNR 210 (34-34-37.452N 120-38-50.146W) - the modern post light at the station site; original 1901 tower location precision 'place'
lights.first_lit: 1901: 'In 1901, the lighthouse service built a light station at Point Arguello' (USCG Historian's Office). The customary day, 1 March 1901, is tertiary-level in this survey.
lights.established_structures: 1901 lighthouse (original tower later removed); by 1968 the station showed a 36-inch rotating aerobeacon of 1,100,000 cp on a structure 124 ft above the water, with two-tone diaphone and radiobeacon (USCG 1968 description; photo captions distinguish 'the original Point Arguello light tower' and 'the Point Arguello skeleton tower'). Today a post light (Light List).
lights.optic: Original apparatus not verified in located sources (commonly given as a fourth-order Fresnel - tertiary only).
lights.why_built: The 'Graveyard of the Pacific' at the west entrance of the Santa Barbara Channel: the Yankee Blade wrecked there 1 October 1854 with about 415 lives and a bullion cargo, and shipwrecks continued for half a century before the 1901 station (USCG narrative). The same rocks later claimed seven destroyers and 22 men in the Honda Point disaster of 8 September 1923 (USCG narrative gives September 9).
lights.automated: 1966-era remote operation implied; explicit automation year not verified (USCG page's structured block is empty for Arguello).
lights.deactivated: Never as a station site; the aid persists as a post light (Light List 2025, Fl W 15s). The 1901 tower itself is gone (replacement commonly dated 1934 - tertiary).
lights.fate: Original structures removed; site within Vandenberg Space Force Base; modern minor aid remains.
lights.nrhp: Not listed (not in NRIS dataset).
lights.keepers_note: The station doubled as a key synoptic weather reporting point for national weather maps, and its associated Coast Guard lifeboat station (est. 1934-38) served until 1958 (USCG).
lights.summary: Point Arguello, where the Yankee Blade went down in 1854 and seven Navy destroyers piled up at Honda Point in 1923, got its light station only in 1901. The original lighthouse gave way in the 1930s to a rotating aerobeacon, and today a simple post light on the Vandenberg coast carries on the station's warning at the west door of the Santa Barbara Channel.

lights.name: Point Conception Light Station
alt_names: Punta de la Limpia Concepcion Light
lights.coord_source: US Coast Guard Light List Vol. VI 2025, LLNR 200 (34-26-55.063N 120-28-14.574W)
lights.first_lit: First lighted 1 February 1856 (NRHP nomination 81000176 narrative: the PIERCE delivered lens and lamp and the light was exhibited 'February 1, 1856'); lower replacement tower first lit 1882 (USCG: established 1856, current tower 1881-82).
lights.established_structures: 1856 tower and dwelling high on the bluff (razed; the nomination notes the original 1854-era lighthouse site presumably destroyed with 1960s razing of buildings); station relocated 1881 to a mesa 133 ft above the sea and the present tower lit 1882 after the Fort Tejon earthquake of 9 January 1857 had earlier damaged the first building (USCG narrative, which misdates the quake to 1867).
lights.optic: First-order Fresnel, 1856, still in use at the time of listing ('still utilizes its original lens,' nomination; USCG concurs 'FIRST ORDER, FRESNEL 1856').
lights.why_built: The 'Cape Horn of the Pacific' - the great turning point between the coastwise route and the Santa Barbara Channel, part of the first 1850s cohort; the lens and ironwork came around Cape Horn from France at a cost of $65,068 (USCG).
lights.deactivated: Never; active (Light List 2025, Fl W 30s).
lights.fate: Standing; active USCG aid on private ranch coast (access restricted).
lights.summary: One of the original eight Pacific lighthouses, Point Conception first showed its French first-order light on 1 February 1856 at the hinge of the California coast. The station moved partway down its bluff in 1881-82 to escape the high fog, and the 1882 tower still turns the 1856 lens - among the longest-serving optics in the country. It was automated in 1973 and remains active.

lights.established_structures: 1926 cylindrical reinforced-concrete tower, 67 ft, on a 130-ft cliff, with Spanish Revival station buildings (USCG; MPS 1920s Spanish Revival grouping; NRHP nomination 80000808, 'Light, built in 1926').

lights.name: Point Fermin Light Station
lights.coord_source: NPS NRHP GIS point for listing 72000234 (33.70534,-118.29366; the historic building at 805 Paseo Del Mar). The modern Point Fermin Light aid (LLNR 140, on pile) is at 33-42-17.310N 118-17-38.408W.
lights.first_lit: 1874 (USCG: established/first lit 1874, 'built in 1874 with lumber from California redwoods'; the 1889 Coast Pilot shows the light in service). The customary day, 15 December 1874, is tertiary-level here.
lights.established_structures: 1874 Stick/Eastlake combination tower-residence, from the same plans as Point Hueneme (first) and East Brother (MPS); lantern room and gallery removed 1942 for a WWII lookout shack; new lantern room and gallery rebuilt 1974 (USCG).
lights.optic: Fourth-order Fresnel, 1874 (USCG).
lights.why_built: Marked San Pedro Bay and the growing port of Los Angeles at Point Fermin's 100-ft bluff (Coast Pilot 1889; MPS harbor-growth context).
lights.automated: Not applicable - extinguished instead (USCG table: 'Automated? N/A').
lights.deactivated: Light extinguished 1941 and lantern removed (USCG narrative; table says deactivated 1942).
lights.fate: Standing in Point Fermin Park, San Pedro; long the park superintendent's residence, now restored with its 1974 lantern (USCG); a separate modern pile light serves mariners nearby (Light List 2025).
lights.keepers_note: Its first keepers were the sisters Mary and Ella Smith (commonly reported - tertiary, not verified in located sources).
lights.summary: Point Fermin's gingerbread redwood lighthouse of 1874, twin to Hueneme's and East Brother's, watched over San Pedro Bay as Los Angeles built its great harbor below. Blacked out days after Pearl Harbor and stripped of its lantern for a lookout shack, it regained a rebuilt lantern room in 1974 and presides over a city park, while a plain pile light does its old job.

lights.name: Los Angeles Harbor Light Station (Angels Gate)
lights.coord_source: US Coast Guard Light List Vol. VI 2025, LLNR 135 (33-42-30.810N 118-15-05.984W)
lights.first_lit: 1913 (USCG: established/first lit 1913; NRHP nomination 80000810: built 'in 1913 at a total cost of $35,971.49'; a temporary light had stood on the breakwater block since its 1910 completion, USCG). The customary day, 1 March 1913, is tertiary-level here.
lights.established_structures: 1913 cylindrical steel-and-concrete tower with black vertical stripes on a 40-ft concrete block at the end of the San Pedro breakwater - a one-off Beaux-Arts design ('the only lighthouse ever built to this design,' USCG); storm-settled with a permanent shoreward list.
lights.optic: Fourth-order Fresnel, 1913 (USCG).
lights.why_built: Purpose-built gateway light for the new Los Angeles breakwater and harbor project planned from 1907 (USCG narrative).
lights.automated: 1 February 1973 ('the station was automated and the keepers departed,' USCG; the table says 1971 - conflict noted).
lights.deactivated: Never; active (Light List 2025, Fl G 15s, continuous horn).
lights.fate: Standing; maintained from Coast Guard Base Terminal Island (USCG).
lights.keepers_note: One night a keeper was knocked to the floor when a blacked-out battleship struck the breakwater beside the tower; the incident was stamped confidential and buried in Navy files for years (USCG narrative). Locals mourned when 'Moaning Maggie,' the two-tone fog horn, was replaced in 1959 by the shriller 'Blatting Betty.'
lights.summary: 'Angels Gate' has stood at the end of the San Pedro breakwater since 1913, a Romanesque concrete cylinder that survived a five-day storm with nothing worse than a permanent lean. Its green flash and foghorns - Moaning Maggie, then Blatting Betty - defined the harbor entrance of Los Angeles; the keepers left on 1 February 1973 when the light was automated.

lights.name: Ballast Point Light Station
alt_names: Ballast Point Lighthouse, San Diego Bay
lights.coord_source: USGS GNIS DomesticNames_CA, feature 238941 'Ballast Point' (Cape, San Diego County); the modern Ballast Point Light B (LLNR 1570) is at 32-41-10.800N 117-13-58.027W
lights.first_lit: 1890: 'In 1890, Ballast Point Lighthouse was constructed' (USCG Historian's Office, article by PhM1 Harmon Lougher). The customary day, 1 August 1890, is tertiary-level here.
lights.established_structures: 1890 pair of dwellings and a white square tower integral with the keeper's quarters, of the Stick-style 1890 trio with San Luis Obispo and Table Bluff (MPS); dwellings torn down and the unstable brick-founded tower demolished around 1960, the light moving to the fog-signal building roof on 5 August of that year (USCG narrative, written contemporaneously).
lights.optic: Fifth-order fixed Fresnel with a green shade, focal height 34 ft; it was 'the last lighthouse displaying a fixed light on the Pacific Coast,' and the lantern and lens went to Cabrillo National Monument (USCG narrative).
lights.why_built: Harbor entrance light inside Point Loma for San Diego Bay, on the historic anchorage where Cabrillo landed in 1542 and whalers later tried out blubber (USCG narrative).
lights.automated: Station kept resident personnel into the 1960s; automation of the successor aid not separately dated in located sources.
lights.deactivated: Historic lighthouse demolished c. 1960; the point remains lit by a minor aid (Light List 2025, Ballast Point Light B, Fl W 4s).
lights.fate: Demolished c. 1960; site within Naval Base Point Loma; lens preserved at Cabrillo National Monument (USCG).
lights.nrhp: Not listed (not in NRIS dataset).
lights.summary: Ballast Point's 1890 Stick-style lighthouse guarded the inner entrance of San Diego Bay from the spit where Cabrillo had anchored in 1542. Its green-shaded fifth-order lens was the Pacific coast's last fixed classical light; when the failing tower came down around 1960 the optic went to Cabrillo National Monument and a utilitarian light took over the point.

lights.name: Old Point Loma Lighthouse
lights.coord_source: NPS NRHP GIS point for listing 74000350 (Old Point Loma Lighthouse, Cabrillo National Monument)
lights.first_lit: 15 November 1855: 'Point Loma Lighthouse was put into service on November 15, 1855' (NPS Cabrillo NM webpage; USCG concurs: 'First lighted November 15, 1855').
lights.established_structures: Structure completed 1854 (architect Ammi B. Young, Treasury Dept.; contractors Gibbons & Kelly, Baltimore); sandstone/brick Cape Cod dwelling with central tower at 422-462 ft elevation - at the time the highest light in the U.S.; restored by the NPS 1933-35 (USCG; NPS; nomination notes 3rd-order lens installed November 1855).
lights.optic: Third-order fixed Fresnel from Sautter & Co., Paris, $3,810 - the lens originally intended for Humboldt Harbor (USCG page).
lights.why_built: First lighthouse of Southern California, in the initial 1850s Pacific cohort, marking San Diego Bay; sited too high, 'too often, its light was obscured by fog and low clouds' (NPS Cabrillo).
lights.automated: Never; replaced.
lights.deactivated: 23 March 1891, when the lens was removed and the new lower station took over (USCG; NPS: 'A new Point Loma Light Station was established at a lower elevation in March 1891').
lights.fate: Preserved centerpiece of Cabrillo National Monument (proclaimed 1913); restored 1933-35; displays a third-order lens (NPS; USCG).
lights.keepers_note: Robert Israel kept the old light for 18 years and personally lit the new station's kerosene lamp on 23 March 1891, serving one more year there (NPS Cabrillo NM page).
lights.summary: The 1855 Old Point Loma light crowned its headland so high that fog regularly blotted it out, an elegant failure of the first Pacific cohort. Extinguished on 23 March 1891 in favor of the new tower at the point's tip, it was saved by its inclusion in Cabrillo National Monument and a 1930s restoration, and is now among the most-visited lighthouses in the country.

lights.name: New Point Loma Lighthouse (Point Loma Light)
lights.coord_source: US Coast Guard Light List Vol. VI 2025, LLNR 5 (32-39-54.258N 117-14-33.601W)
lights.first_lit: 23 March 1891: 'The new Point Loma Light Station, established on March 23, 1891,' with keeper Robert Israel lighting the kerosene lamp (NPS Cabrillo NM page; USCG concurs on 1891).
lights.established_structures: 1891 iron/steel skeleton tower with central stair cylinder at the low tip of Point Loma, 88 ft above the water, with fog-signal building at its base and keepers' dwellings (USCG; MPS cites it among prefabricated-metal innovations).
lights.optic: Third-order Fresnel, 1891, showing alternating red and white via ruby glass screens until 1912, then a single white flash every 15 seconds; historic lens removed 2001 and displayed at the monument's Assistant Keepers Quarters (NPS; USCG).
lights.why_built: Replaced the fog-plagued 1855 hilltop light with a sea-level light at the harbor entrance (NPS Cabrillo).
lights.automated: 1973 (USCG table).
lights.deactivated: Never; active (Light List 2025, Fl W 15s, 'Black house on white square pyramidal skeleton tower').
lights.fate: Standing; active USCG aid beside Cabrillo National Monument; not individually NRHP-listed.
lights.nrhp: Not found in the NRIS listed-properties dataset as an individual listing.
lights.keepers_note: Robert Israel, the old light's last keeper, lit the new lamp on opening night, 23 March 1891 (NPS).
lights.summary: The skeletal 1891 tower at the foot of Point Loma corrected its predecessor's fatal elevation, flashing red and white over the harbor entrance until 1912 and plain white ever since. Automated in 1973 and stripped of its classical lens in 2001, the black-and-white ironwork remains San Diego's working sea light.

lights.name: San Francisco Lightship Station
lights.coord_source: Position of the successor aid, San Francisco Approach Lighted Whistle Buoy SF, Light List Vol. VI 2025, LLNR 360 (37-44-59.761N 122-41-33.995W). Historic station: '8.6 miles and 244 degrees from the Point Bonita Light,' originally '3 1/4 miles outside the bar in 109 feet, with Alcatraz and Fort Point lighthouses in range' (USCG Lightship Station Index).
lights.first_lit: Station established 1898 with LV-70, purpose-built at Portland, Oregon (Wolff & Zwicker Iron Works) under an $80,000 appropriation 'for lightship for San Francisco harbor' (USCG Historian's Office lightship pages).
lights.established_structures: Lightships assigned: LV-70 (1898-1930), LV-83/WAL-508 (1930-1942), station vacant during WWII, LV-83 (1945-1951), WLV-612 (1951-1969), LV-100/WAL-523 (1969-1971) (USCG Lightship Station Index).
lights.optic: LV-70 showed a cluster of three 100-candlepower electric lens lanterns at each masthead - an early electrically lit lightship - with 12-inch steam chime whistle and hand-operated 1,000-lb bell; oil lamps substituted 1900-1904 during generator troubles (USCG LV-70 page).
lights.why_built: 'The station marked the approaches to the main ship channel into San Francisco' outside the bar (USCG Lightship Station Index).
lights.automated: Not applicable; replaced by a large automated buoy.
lights.deactivated: 1971; 'the station was replaced by the San Francisco lighted horn (LNB) buoy "SF"' (USCG).
lights.fate: Station discontinued 1971; today's SF Approach Lighted Whistle Buoy occupies the approach role. LV-70 itself was an experimental wireless-telegraph platform in August 1899 (USCG LV-70 page).
lights.nrhp: Not applicable (station); no listed vessel from this station survives under its SF identity.
lights.keepers_note: In August 1899 LV-70 hosted a 17-day experiment in wireless telegraphy - among the earliest marine radio trials on the Pacific coast (USCG LV-70 page).
lights.summary: From 1898 the San Francisco lightship rode outside the bar where Alcatraz and Fort Point ranged in line, showing masthead electric lanterns to funnel traffic into the Golden Gate's main ship channel. Five vessels held the station over 73 years - LV-70, LV-83, WLV-612 and LV-100 among them - until a lighted horn buoy replaced the last ship in 1971.

lights.name: Blunts Reef Lightship Station
alt_names: Blunt's Reef lightship, off Cape Mendocino
lights.coord_source: Position of Blunts Reef Lighted Bell Buoy 40, Light List Vol. VI 2025, LLNR 485 (40-26-49.048N 124-29-56.772W), which marks the reef; the lightship station lay 'about 1.9 miles and 239 degrees from Blunts Reef and 4.55 miles and 266 degrees from Cape Mendocino Light' (USCG Lightship Station Index)
lights.first_lit: Station established 1905 (USCG Lightship Station Index: 'Blunts Reef, 1905-1971'); the LV-83 vessel page says the ship was 'placed on Blunts Reef (CA) off Cape Mendocino' in 1906 - discrepancy noted.
lights.established_structures: Lightships assigned: LV-83/WAL-508 (1905-1930), LV-100/WAL-523 (1930-1942), buoy during WWII, LV-100 (1945-1959), WLV-605 (1960-1969), WLV-612 (1969-1971) (USCG Station Index).
lights.optic: Lightship illuminating apparatus per vessel; LV-83 (built 1904, Camden NJ) was a steam screw, steel-hulled ship with masthead lights (USCG LV-83 page).
lights.why_built: Guarded Blunts Reef, the outlying rocks off Cape Mendocino inside which coastwise traffic hugged the shore in fog; the 1889 Coast Pilot's directions run 'outside Blunt's Reef, on the range of the south rock of the reef and Cape Mendocino Light.'
lights.automated: Not applicable; replaced by a large automated buoy.
lights.deactivated: 1971; 'replaced by the Blunts Reef Lighted Horn Buoy "B"' (USCG). Today the reef carries Lighted Bell Buoy 40 (Light List 2025).
lights.fate: Station discontinued 1971. WLV-605, which held the station 1960-69, survives as the museum lightship RELIEF at Oakland, NRHP ref 89002462, listed 1989-12-20 (NRIS).
lights.nrhp: Station not listable; associated vessel WLV-605 RELIEF listed 1989 (NRIS 89002462).
lights.keepers_note: On 15 June 1916, between 1:45 and 3:30 a.m., LV-83's crew took aboard 155 people - the passengers and crew of the stranded steamer Bear - in one of the great lightship rescues (USCG LV-83 page). The same ship was dragged off station by storms in November-December 1906.
lights.summary: The Blunts Reef lightship tossed off Cape Mendocino from 1905, holding coastwise traffic clear of the reef that the cape's high light could not adequately cover in fog. LV-83's rescue of 155 souls from the steamer Bear in 1916 made it famous; buoys replaced the ships in 1971, and one veteran of the station, WLV-605 RELIEF, survives on the National Register at Oakland.
